summary:
Bihār has no state-specific transgender legislation. A trans visitor to the state stands directly under India's national framework, and no source material documents a Bihār deviation sufficient to score separately from the national position.

That framework was substantially rewritten in March 2026. India's Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill in both houses; the measure awaits presidential assent. It removes the right to self-identification affirmed by the Supreme Court of India's 2014 judgment recognising transgender people as a third gender, limits legal recognition to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner and to intersex individuals, and mandates medical certification for identity recognition. Self-identified trans men, trans women and non-binary people fall outside the recognition scheme. Human Rights Watch called the bill a major setback that strips thousands of rights and increases risk; the government presents the change as widening access to welfare schemes and protection from trafficking, while critics say it excludes many trans, non-binary and gender-fluid people. Opposition parties and LGBTQ organisations protested. India has an estimated two million transgender people, and even before the amendment recognition was uneven, with continuing discrimination in education, healthcare and formal employment.

The baseline for entry and stay is mixed. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018, and discrimination on grounds including sex has been interpreted by courts to cover gender identity. There is no same-sex marriage or civil partnership.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024. Replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed the gender-identity-specific sexual-violence offences that had protected trans persons from assault, and trans people fear a rise in attacks as a result.

Identity documents and checkpoints are a live source of friction. In February 2026 the Allahabad High Court granted relief to a trans person who had been required to undergo a medical examination by passport authorities. In November 2024 an openly transgender law student, Sakshi Jain, was stopped at Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 by Central Industrial Security Force personnel despite presenting her PAN card for identity verification. In Kolkata a transwoman alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her at the station under the pretext of checking her gender, and transgender people arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam have recounted degrading treatment in custody. None of the documented incidents took place in Bihār, but each involves central forces and agencies that operate in every state.

Assessments of police conduct diverge. The United Kingdom's December 2025 country policy note records limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic; victim interviews documented in June 2024 record abusive treatment of trans detainees by railway police. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police issued sweeping guidelines on protecting LGBTQIA+ persons, police sensitisation and a ban on conversion therapy, with directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities. Those bans coexist with clandestine conversion-therapy networks that continue to operate.
tangentialFactors:
Facilities and welfare infrastructure are set largely at state level, and Bihār is not among the states running a transgender welfare board. Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Maharashtra and Odisha operate such boards coordinating housing subsidies, free sex reassignment surgery in public hospitals and pensions, and several other states provide targeted welfare, housing and healthcare benefits for hijras. A visitor comparing Bihār with those states should expect fewer coordinated state services.

Nationally the Ayushman Bharat scheme was expanded in April 2024 to cover transition-related healthcare for all members of the transgender community, which applies in Bihār as elsewhere. In August 2024 the Ministry of Finance clarified that LGBTQ people face no restrictions on opening joint bank accounts or naming partners as beneficiaries.

Intersex minors remain at risk. Reports document a history of infanticide and a strong parental preference for assigning intersex infants male through non-consensual operations; in April 2019 the Madras High Court ordered the Tamil Nadu government to ban sex-selective surgeries on intersex infants.

outOfScopeNotes:
No source material documents Bihār-specific police conduct toward transgender people, state-level documentation office practice, or any Bihār state welfare scheme for transgender residents. Whether the state runs any targeted programme is unresolved in the sources.

The checkpoint and custody incidents cited here occurred in Tamil Nadu, West Bengal and Assam and under central forces, not in Bihār; their relevance to Bihār rests on the nationwide operation of those agencies rather than on state evidence.

The Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill had not received presidential assent at the time of the sources dated March 2026, so the final form of the recognition regime is unresolved.
